```{r setup, include=FALSE}

```

H1: Those who report a history of infidelity (categorical) will report lower relationship satisfaction/commitment (composite).

H2: Willingness to marry without love will be negatively correlated with age.


## 1. Load the package and data

```{r load, message=FALSE}
#load the codebook package
library(codebook)

#load data/raw/data_doctored.csv
raw <- read.csv("data/raw/data_doctored.csv")

#check row and column counts, inspect the first few rows. Will give number of rows and number of columns. 
dim(raw)
head(raw[,c("ResponseId")])
str(raw) #amount of observations and variables, variables & first values

#make data with ID, age, history of infidelity, willingness to marry without love, and relationship satisfaction/commitment prqc 1-6 unchanged
#codebook has variable names for this dataset
data <- raw[,c("ResponseId",
               "Age",
               "infidelity",
               "Relationship_status",
               "Love_would_you_marry_1",
               "prqc_1",
               "prqc_2",
               "prqc_3",
               "prqc_4",
               "prqc_5",
               "prqc_6")]

#This should now show less variables than before (11) in this case
dim(data)
str(data) #now is more trackable, because it only has the columns we need

```


## 2. Check participant IDs
We want to validate the participant ID, because eg. there can be duplicates (two responses from one participant), or no data at all for a participant 

```{r participant_ids}

#count na. #False is 0, True is 1 --> It will count how many "true" values aka. NA data are there 
sum(is.na(data$ResponseId))

#count blank. (na.rm will remove those that are NA and just leave those that are blank)
sum(data$ResponseId=="",na.rm=TRUE)

#count duplicates. (How many not unique IDs are there)
sum(duplicated(data$ResponseId))

#All these previous can be found out with: 

###JK: There is a small typo in the ID name here. ###
# Replace the line below with:
# summary(data$ResponseId)
###  End of comment ###

summary(data$Response_Id)

#inspect records with missing or blank IDs. Tells you which one is the NA Participant Id in the order of columns.
missingID <- which(is.na(data$ResponseId))
missingID
data[missingID,]
print(data[missingID,]) #we remove row because the particpant has only Nas


#remove the known empty record with no ID, then check the row count
data <- data[!is.na(data$ResponseId),] #! is saying "no"/ It will only leave the things that are not NA
dim(data) #should now display one less participant
```


## 3. Recode Infidelity

```{r infidelity}
# codebook: 0 = No infidelity, 1 = Infidelity
table(data$infidelity, useNA="ifany")
#turn infidelity into a factor with labels No infidelity and Infidelity

data$infidelity <- factor(data$infidelity,
                         levels=c(0,1),
                         labels=c("No Infidelity","Infidelity"))
                         
table(data$infidelity,useNA="ifany")


```

## Make composite relationship satisfaction and commitment [prqc items 1-6]
```{r}
#make relData for respondents currently in a relationship
#include Dating (1), In a committed relationship (2), and Married (3)
table(data$Relationship_status, useNA = "ifany")
relData_try <- data[c(3,4)]
relData <- data[data$Relationship_status %in% c(1,2,3),]
nrow(relData)

#define the items to check; all four use response codes 1-7
#prqc_1-6: 1=Not at all, 7=Extremely
likert7 <- c("prqc_1","prqc_2","prqc_3","prqc_4","prqc_5","prqc_6")

#check the summaries and missing responses
summary(relData[,likert7])
colSums(is.na(relData[,likert7]))

#inspect the response frequencies for each item
for(i in likert7){
  print(i)
  print(table(relData[,i],useNA="ifany"))
}

#replace any codes outside 1-7 with NA
for(i in likert7){
  relData[,i] <- ifelse(relData[,i] %in% 1:7,relData[,i],NA)
}

```
## Calculate satisfaction/commitment (new)
```{r satisfaction/commitment}
#group commitment variables (prqc_1:6)
#these ask how satisfied, committed, dedicated, and devoted respondents are
#none requires reverse coding
satcomVars <- c("prqc_1","prqc_2","prqc_3","prqc_4","prqc_5","prqc_6")


###JK: Your calculation uses six items, so please change "all three items" below to "available responses across the six items." ###

#calculate satisfaction/commitment as the mean of all three items
#for NAs, conduct available item mean
relData$satisfaction_commitment <- rowMeans(relData[,satcomVars],na.rm=TRUE)

#check the score
summary(relData$satisfaction_commitment)

#make h1Data with ID, history of infidelity, satisfaction/commitment
#keep participants with both hist of infidelity and satisfaction/commitment present
#do not apply the H1 preference filter to this hypothesis
h1Data <- relData[!is.na(relData$infidelity) & !is.na(relData$satisfaction_commitment),
                  c("ResponseId","infidelity","satisfaction_commitment")]
```

HYPOTHESIS 2: Willingness to marry without love will be negatively correlated with age
```{r check age and willingness to marry}
#count na: 9754
sum(is.na(data$Age))

#count blank: 0
sum(data$Age=="",na.rm=T)

#check that each age is reasonable 18-99
summary(data$Age)

#count na: 16060
sum(is.na(data$Love_would_you_marry_1))

#count blank: 0
sum(data$Love_would_you_marry_1=="",na.rm=T)

###JK: This check is for willingness to marry without love, not age. ###
# Please change the comment below to say that the expected range is 0-100.
# For the age check earlier, the codebook range is 18-90, not 18-99.
###  End of comment ###

#check that each age is reasonable 18-99
summary(data$Love_would_you_marry_1)

```

## 5. age & willingness to marry without love
```{r hypothesis 2}
#make h2Data with ID, age, and willingness to marry without love
#keep participants with both age and willingness to marry without love present

h2Data <- data[!is.na(data$Age) & !is.na(data$Love_would_you_marry_1),
                  c("ResponseId",
                  "Age",
                  "Love_would_you_marry_1")]

```

## 7. Check the final tables

```{r final_tables}
#check rows, columns, types, and missing values in h1Data
#one row per participant, one column per variable
dim(h1Data)
str(h1Data)
head(h1Data)
colSums(is.na(h1Data))
table(h1Data$infidelity,useNA="ifany")
range(h1Data$satisfaction_commitment)
sum(duplicated(h1Data$ResponseId))

#repeat the checks for h2Data; age 18-90, marry without love 0-100
dim(h2Data)
str(h2Data)
head(h2Data)
colSums(is.na(h2Data))
range(h2Data$Age)
range(h2Data$Love_would_you_marry_1)
sum(duplicated(h2Data$ResponseId))
```

## 8. Add labels and generate codebooks

The descriptions come from the original codebook and our scoring decisions.
`compact_codebook()` adds summaries from the actual data. Knit the Rmd to
display the formatted codebooks.

```{r variable_labels}
#add a description to each h1Data column, in column order
#include the source codes, meaning, and units
###JK: Please make the codebook descriptions a little more specific, following Section 8 of my Lab03 example. ###
# You can replace the infidelity label below with:
# "History of sexual or emotional infidelity to a romantic partner: original codes 0=No, 1=Yes; stored as a factor."
# In the H2 labels, give the age unit and the willingness scale anchors:
# var_label(h2Data) <- c(
#   "Unique participant ID (ResponseId)",
#   "Age in years; questionnaire range 18-90.",
#   "Willingness to marry or register a partnership with a desirable person one does not love: 0=Definitely would not, 100=Definitely would."
# )
###  End of comment ###

var_label(h1Data) <- c(
  "Unique participant ID (ResponseId)",
  "History of infidelity",
  "Relationship satisfaction/commitment: mean of available prqc_1-6 responses, each 1=Not at all to 7=Extremely;"
)

#add a description to each h2Data column, in column order
#include response anchors and the commitment scoring rule
var_label(h2Data) <- c(
  "Unique participant ID (ResponseId)",
  "Age",
  "Would you marry without love (Love_would_you_marry_1)")
```

H1 includes participants with an ID, whether they have a history of infidelity, and a composite of their relationship satisfaction and commitment (prqc 1:6) Factor level numbers in the
generated table are internal R positions, not the original survey codes.

```{r h1_codebook}
#generate the h1Data codebook
compact_codebook(h1Data)

```

H2 includes participants with an ID, relationship status 1, 2, or 3, and
valid nonmissing qoa and at least one valid commitment response.

```{r h2_codebook}
###JK: Please replace the H2 inclusion description above; it still refers to the example's qoa and commitment variables. ###
# Your H2 correctly uses age and willingness to marry without love, and it does not restrict participants to relationship statuses 1, 2, and 3.
# Suggested wording: H2 includes participants with an ID and nonmissing age and willingness-to-marry-without-love responses, regardless of relationship status.
###  End of comment ###

#generate the h2Data codebook
compact_codebook(h2Data)

```

## 9. Save the final tables

```{r save}
#create data/processed_data if needed
dir.create("data/processed_data",recursive=T,showWarnings=F)

#save h1Data and h2Data without an extra row-number column
write.csv(h1Data,"data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv",row.names=F)
write.csv(h2Data,"data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv",row.names=F)

#read the files back and confirm their dimensions
h1Saved <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h1.csv")
h2Saved <- read.csv("data/processed_data/practice_h2.csv")
dim(h1Saved)
dim(h2Saved)

```
